Content:
The conditional statement [MATH: A \Rightarrow B] is logically equivalent to the disjunction [MATH: \lnot A \lor B{:}]

Content:
[MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \lnot A \lor B]

Content:
We can verify this by the following truth table:

Content:
| [MATH: \,A\,] | [MATH: \,B\,] | [MATH: \, A \Rightarrow B \,] | [MATH: \, \neg A \lor B \,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm F] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] |

Content:
In other words, any conditional statement of the form

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] if antecedent, then consequent

Content:
can be expressed equivalently as

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] not antecedent, or consequent.

Content:
For example, consider the following conditional statement:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] If you do not take your watch, then you will be late for the meeting.

Content:
Let's rewrite this statement using its logically equivalent form.

Content:
First, we denote the antecedent [MATH: A] and consequent [MATH: B] as follows:

Content:
- [MATH: A{:}] You do not take your watch.
- [MATH: B{:}] You will be late for the meeting.

Content:
Then, our initial statement can be written as [MATH: A \Rightarrow B,] which is logically equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: \neg A \lor B.]

Content:
The negation of [MATH: A] is:

Content:
- [MATH: \neg A{:}] You take your watch.

Content:
Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] You take your watch, or you will be late for the meeting.

Content:
We can write this using more everyday language as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] Take your watch, or you will be late for the meeting.

Content:
Another way to write this is to append the word "either" to the beginning of the sentence, like so:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] Either you take your watch, or you will be late for the meeting.

Content:
Using the word "either" helps clarify that the sentence structure presents two alternatives and is particularly useful when employing the disjunctive form [MATH: (\lnot A\lor B)] in conversational or formal English. So, the phrase effectively conveys that one of the two stated conditions will hold true.

sections.normalized_html:
Which statement is logically equivalent to the following conditional statement?

[MATH: \qquad] If you take an umbrella, then you will stay dry.
sections.readable_text:
Which statement is logically equivalent to the following conditional statement?

[MATH: \qquad] If you take an umbrella, then you will stay dry.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's denote by [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] the following statements:

  • [MATH: A{:}] You take an umbrella.

  • [MATH: B{:}] You will stay dry.

Then, our initial statement can be written as [MATH: A \Rightarrow B,] which is logically equivalent to

[MATH: \neg A \lor B.]

The negation of [MATH: A] can be written as

  • [MATH: \neg A{:}] You do not take an umbrella.

Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

[MATH: \qquad] You do not take an umbrella, or you will stay dry.

We can write this in more everyday language as follows:

[MATH: \qquad] Either you do not take an umbrella, or you will stay dry.

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: X \Rightarrow \neg Y \equiv \neg (X \land Y)]
2. [MATH: \neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right)\equiv \neg X \land Y]
3. [MATH: \neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right)\equiv X \land Y]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine each of our statements:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, [MATH: X \Rightarrow \neg Y] is logically equivalent to the disjunction [MATH: \neg X \lor \neg Y,] which by De Morgan's law is equivalent to [MATH: \neg (X\land Y).]
- Statement III is true, while statement II is false. From part I, we have the following equivalence:
[MATH: X \Rightarrow \neg Y\equiv \neg (X\land Y)]
By negating this statement, we get
[MATH: \neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right) \equiv \neg \left(\neg (X\land Y)\right).]
Canceling out double negation, we reach
[MATH: X\land Y.]
So, [MATH: \neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right)] is equivalent to [MATH: X \land Y.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

sections.normalized_html: Simplify the statement [MATH: \neg (A \Rightarrow \neg B) \lor A.]
sections.readable_text: Simplify the statement [MATH: \neg (A \Rightarrow \neg B) \lor A.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, note that the conditional statement [MATH: A \Rightarrow eg B] is logically equivalent to the disjunction [MATH: \lnot A \lor eg B.] So, we have

[MATH: eg (A \Rightarrow eg B) \lor A \equiv eg ( eg A \lor eg B) \lor A.]

Now, we can distribute the negation over the disjunction using De Morgan's law:

[MATH: eg ( eg A \lor eg B) \lor A \equiv ( eg ( eg A) \land eg ( eg B) ) \lor A]

Canceling out double negations, we reach [MATH: ( eg ( eg A) \land eg ( eg B) ) \lor A \equiv (A \land B) \lor A.]

Finally, by the absorption law, we have

[MATH: (A \land B) \lor A \equiv A.]

So the given statement is equivalent to [MATH: A.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The conditional statement [MATH: A \Rightarrow B] is logically equivalent to the disjunction [MATH: \lnot A \lor B{:}]

Content:
[MATH: A \Rightarrow B \equiv \lnot A \lor B]

Content:
We can verify this by the following truth table:

Content:
| [MATH: \,A\,] | [MATH: \,B\,] | [MATH: \, A \Rightarrow B \,] | [MATH: \, \neg A \lor B \,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm F] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{blue} \textrm T] |

Content:
In other words, any conditional statement of the form

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] if antecedent, then consequent

Content:
can be expressed equivalently as

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] not antecedent, or consequent.

Content:
For example, consider the following conditional statement:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] If you do not take your watch, then you will be late for the meeting.

Content:
Let's rewrite this statement using its logically equivalent form.

Content:
First, we denote the antecedent [MATH: A] and consequent [MATH: B] as follows:

Content:
- [MATH: A{:}] You do not take your watch.
- [MATH: B{:}] You will be late for the meeting.

Content:
Then, our initial statement can be written as [MATH: A \Rightarrow B,] which is logically equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: \neg A \lor B.]

Content:
The negation of [MATH: A] is:

Content:
- [MATH: \neg A{:}] You take your watch.

Content:
Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] You take your watch, or you will be late for the meeting.

Content:
We can write this using more everyday language as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] Take your watch, or you will be late for the meeting.

Content:
Another way to write this is to append the word "either" to the beginning of the sentence, like so:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] Either you take your watch, or you will be late for the meeting.

Content:
Using the word "either" helps clarify that the sentence structure presents two alternatives and is particularly useful when employing the disjunctive form [MATH: (\lnot A\lor B)] in conversational or formal English. So, the phrase effectively conveys that one of the two stated conditions will hold true.

---

Item 2 — Example: Expressing Conditional Statements as Disjunctions

Example Prompt:
Which statement is logically equivalent to the following conditional statement?

[MATH: \qquad] If you take an umbrella, then you will stay dry.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's denote by [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] the following statements:

- [MATH: A{:}] You take an umbrella.
- [MATH: B{:}] You will stay dry.

Then, our initial statement can be written as [MATH: A \Rightarrow B,] which is logically equivalent to

[MATH: \neg A \lor B.]

The negation of [MATH: A] can be written as

- [MATH: \neg A{:}] You do not take an umbrella.

Therefore, the given statement is logically equivalent to the following:

[MATH: \qquad] You do not take an umbrella, or you will stay dry.

We can write this in more everyday language as follows:

[MATH: \qquad] Either you do not take an umbrella, or you will stay dry.

- [MATH: B{:}] You will get sunburn.

Then, our initial statement can be written as [MATH: A \lor B,] which is logically equivalent to

The negation of [MATH: A] can be written as

Item 8 — Example: Rewriting Symbolic Conditional Statements

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: X \Rightarrow \neg Y \equiv \neg (X \land Y)]
2. [MATH: \neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right)\equiv \neg X \land Y]
3. [MATH: \neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right)\equiv X \land Y]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine each of our statements:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, [MATH: X \Rightarrow \neg Y] is logically equivalent to the disjunction [MATH: \neg X \lor \neg Y,] which by De Morgan's law is equivalent to [MATH: \neg (X\land Y).]
- Statement III is true, while statement II is false. From part I, we have the following equivalence:
[MATH: X \Rightarrow \neg Y\equiv \neg (X\land Y)]
By negating this statement, we get
[MATH: \neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right) \equiv \neg \left(\neg (X\land Y)\right).]
Canceling out double negation, we reach
[MATH: X\land Y.]
So, [MATH: \neg \left(X \Rightarrow \neg Y\right)] is equivalent to [MATH: X \land Y.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."
